cases.description: Complete robotic-control project in a domain not represented by a hard-coded stream.
text:
## 1. Objective
The gripper had to hold flexible parts with less than 3 mm deformation and no more than 4% slip during a 40-second transfer.

## 2. Starting point
The existing fixed-force controller produced 11 mm deformation. Supplier force tables could not predict deformation when part stiffness varied within a batch.

## 3. Uncertainty
The team did not know whether pressure distribution inferred from motor current could control grip force before visible deformation occurred.

## 4. Standard limitation
Standard force feedback was insufficient because identical total force produced different local deformation on parts with different stiffness distributions.

## 5. Hypothesis
The team expected a current-gradient signal to identify the onset of local deformation.

## 6. Tests
The team tested five current filters and four force-update intervals. Two filters reacted too late and produced more than 8 mm deformation. A fast filter reduced deformation to 4 mm but caused 7% slip.

## 7. Pivot
The team compared three distributed pressure-estimation models and refined the force update. The selected combination produced 2.6 mm deformation and 3.2% slip in 38 seconds.

## 11. Records
Motor-current traces, force logs, camera measurements, model versions, test matrices, and engineering notes recorded each alternative and decision.

## 13. Knowledge
The team determined that total motor current was not viable because different stiffness distributions produced the same aggregate signal. Current gradients established an earlier indicator of local deformation.

## 14. Boundary
The selected method established 2.6 mm deformation and 3.2% slip for the tested stiffness range.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Parts with discontinuous internal reinforcement remained technologically uncertain at fiscal year-end.

cases.description: Complete qualitative investigation using morphology and fracture observations rather than numeric thresholds.
text:
## 1. Objective
Acceptance required a continuous ceramic edge, no branching fracture after firing, and full bonding at the insert interface.

## 2. Starting method
The supplier firing sequence produced branching edge fractures and separation at the insert.

## 3. Uncertainty
It was unknown whether binder staging could preserve both edge continuity and insert bonding during firing.

## 4. Standard limitation
Published firing guidance was insufficient because it did not address the competing shrinkage directions around the insert.

## 5. Theory
The team expected staged binder removal to prevent the early edge fracture.

## 6. Trials
Several removal sequences and hold stages were tested against standard-sequence controls. Early removal prevented insert separation but formed a branching edge fracture. Late removal preserved the edge but caused complete insert separation.

## 7. Further trial
A split removal stage produced a continuous edge and retained insert bonding after firing. The observation was repeated on separate batches.

## 11. Evidence
Batch sheets, labelled fracture images, microscopy notes, sequence versions, and witness records documented the controls and alternatives.

## 13. Findings
The team determined that neither early nor late removal was viable because each concentrated shrinkage at a different interface. Split removal controlled the competing fracture paths.

## 16. Open boundary
Behaviour with inserts containing internal channels remained technologically uncertain at year-end.

text:
## 1. Objective
The system targeted 96% classification accuracy and latency below 70 ms.

## 3. Uncertainty
The team did not know whether temporal features could meet both targets.

## 5. Hypothesis
The team expected a temporal model to improve accuracy.

## 6. Tests
The team tested multiple sequence lengths and four model configurations. Two failed below 85% and were abandoned. The selected model reached 96.4% and 66 ms.

## 11. Records
Test matrices, datasets, model versions, logs, and commits recorded the experiments.

## 13. Knowledge
The team determined that short event order was required because static features merged the classes.

## 14. Boundary
The tested model established 96.4% accuracy and 66 ms on the reference distribution.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Unseen event combinations remained technologically uncertain at year-end.

cases.description: Standard cloud migration work with extensive testing and metrics but no technological uncertainty.
text:
## 1. Goal
The company migrated reports to an off-the-shelf cloud warehouse with refresh under 15 minutes.

## 2. Available method
Vendor documentation specified the supported migration utility, schema mapping, and scaling settings.

## 3. Work
The team configured the documented utility and tested several standard warehouse sizes. The medium setting refreshed reports in 12 minutes and was selected.

## 4. Validation
Standard reconciliation queries showed 100% row-count agreement. No custom algorithm, unresolved technological uncertainty, or experimental advancement was involved.

## 11. Records
Migration tickets, vendor support notes, configuration exports, and validation logs documented the implementation.

cases.description: Otherwise complete evidence with conflicting statements about whether the experiments occurred in the claimed year.
text:
## 1. Objective
The controller targeted drift below 2% and response below 20 ms during fiscal 2025.

## 2. Starting technology
The existing controller produced 8% drift. Standard compensation failed after rapid load changes.

## 3. Uncertainty
The team did not know whether load-history compensation could meet both targets.

## 5. Hypothesis
The team expected a history model to reduce drift.

## 6. Fiscal-year work
The narrative states that five models were tested between March and October 2025. Two failed above 5% drift. The selected model reached 1.8% drift and 18 ms.

## 11. Records
Model versions, test logs, load traces, and commits record each iteration. The attached project ledger states that all experiments actually began in February 2026 and that no experimental work occurred in 2025.

## 13. Knowledge
The team determined that load history was required because identical current loads followed different drift paths.

## 14. Boundary
The method established 1.8% drift and 18 ms under the reference load sequence.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Abrupt reverse loading remained technologically uncertain at year-end.

## 1. Objective
The detector targeted 91% recall and false alarms below 5%.

## 2. Starting technology
The existing method reached 63% recall, and standard threshold tuning could not exceed 68%.

## 3. Uncertainty
The team did not know whether event-sequence features could meet both targets.

## 5. Hypothesis
The team expected sequence features to separate the events.

## 6. Experiments
Several windows and three classifiers were tested. Two failed below 80% recall. The selected model reportedly reached 92% recall and 4.4% false alarms.

## 11. Evidence status
Test logs and dataset versions are referenced in the summary, but the files are unavailable and cannot be produced. No source commit can be tied to the reported result.

## 13. Knowledge
The team determined that event order was required because static peaks overlapped.

## 14. Boundary
The reported model reached 92% recall and 4.4% false alarms on reference data.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Overlapping events remained technologically uncertain at year-end.

cases.description: Complete project where one stream matches known software vocabulary and another is an unseen fluid-control domain.
text:
## 1. Objective
The dosing system had to keep mixture variation below 2% while software response remained below 25 ms across flow from 10 to 80 litres per minute.

## 2. Starting technology
The fixed valve geometry produced 9% mixture variation. The polling controller produced 48 ms response. Supplier sizing equations could not predict recirculation during fast valve changes.

## 3. Uncertainties
The team did not know whether staged valve geometry could suppress recirculation or whether an event-driven queue could maintain response without destabilizing flow control.

## 4. Standard limitations
Standard valve sizing was insufficient because transient recirculation reversed the concentration gradient. Standard polling could not meet 25 ms.

## 5. Hypotheses
The team expected staged valve inserts and a bounded event queue to meet the targets.

## 6. Fluid tests
Four insert geometries and five valve sequences were tested. Two geometries increased recirculation and were abandoned. The staged insert reduced variation to 2.7%.

## 7. Software tests
Three queue designs were compared. The fastest reached 18 ms but destabilized valve updates.

## 8. Integrated pivot
A synchronized insert sequence and bounded queue reached 1.8% mixture variation and 22 ms response.

## 11. Records
Flow traces, concentration measurements, queue logs, geometry files, test matrices, commits, and decision notes recorded all alternatives.

## 13. Knowledge
The team determined that steady-state valve sizing was not viable because transient recirculation dominated mixing. It established that queue and valve state had to be bounded together.

## 14. Boundary
The integrated method established 1.8% variation and 22 ms across the tested flow range.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Operation with gas entrainment remained technologically uncertain at year-end.
